> @zkabelac says DM devices without target devices cannot exist (see earlier PR). Can you explain please how you ran into this and created a DM device in this way?

There are 3 steps to create a DM device.  1 Create device ->  2 Load table -> 3 Resume table.  I guess the creation is broken after step2 when reboot.  We can use gdb to construct this DM device.

Codewise looks fine to me, but I'd really like to understand this first, i.e. how come you have this DM device without any target? As mentioned @zkabelac suggests this should not be a reachable state. Can you explain?

Also, would love some blessing from @zkabelac/@oniko/@mbroz that this is the right thing to do for our use case. (Summary of the usecase: this is the safety net if the first phase of the shutdown didn't detach things correctly. Here detaching everything that is left, with some "middle ground" data safety guarantees, i.e. sync what is in flight but otherwise don't be too concerned, with getting everything into entirely clean order, we want to be robust here, and somewhat dumb).

As @lixiaokeng say, broken after step 1, the DM device be a unreachable state; broken after step 2, the DM device has target, but mapped_device->map (in kernel code) is null, kernel will hung if reboot now, the mapped_device->map will assign in resume.

This would be a bug in DM target kernel code -   DM device without table line simply does not have /dev/dm-XXX  accessible device node.
So if you know the reproducer for this case - report this on  dm-devel list.

Looking at the original description of this issue -   it looks like the analysis of the vm core  was not finding proper root cause here - since device without  DM table line does not have  /dev/dm-xxx entry - so user cannot open such device - and cannot send any 'sync' to such device. 

So what we really need to see  (if its   DM/lvm2 involved here)  is a reproducer for this case - how to reproduce such shutdown scenario.

This looks like faulty test case,

You may not 'stop' lvm2 command in the middle of DM processing (table manipulation) - since  lvm2  command holds  'so called' VG lock - so if your 'gdb' stops it inside the VG locked section - no other lvm2 command will be able to do anything - so no deactivation by any other lvm2 command is possible  (only dmsetup remove would work)

If you want to check what is doing 'empty' unloaded DM  device - just use  something like: 'dmsetup create --notable  testdevice'

> I just use gdb to reproduce this case, actually, the dm device create by docker in testcase, and execute reboot command in the middle of DM processing.

There needs to be known full sequence - this doesn't look like kernel bug at all - it's most likely some 'app' waiting blocked on some lock to proceed.

It's worth to be noted LVM does not support 'containers' - DM (or block devices as whole) are not containerized resource - and the lvm2 create work with system udevd  to synchronize its operation - it  'container' instance doesn't have working 'udev'  - lvm2 is getting stuck waiting on semaphore (which is normally managed by udevd).

There are some ways how to make things a bit more 'movable'  - i.e. disabling udev synchronization - but it's still non-trivial without good understanding.

My best guess is - the  DM device is simply holding IO and is not properly deactivated  - for better analysis is usually  good  Alt+F9 systemd debug shell - that can reveal which process is blocking progress.

It's not clear which version of lvm2 is here in use - relatively recently we've slightly improved shutdown support for 'dmeventd' monitoring - that used to often 'block'  the shutdown.

> During the shutdown process，the systemd-shutdown process will be the process 1 and send the SIGTERM and SIGKILL signal to all the process remaining for cleaning. This may cause the command stopped in the middle of DM processing (maybe table manipulation) and the systemd-shutdown will suspended all the time if we use fsync before detach DM device. This PR is used to solve this kind of problem.

During the shutdown process，the systemd-shutdown process will be the process 1 and send the SIGTERM and SIGKILL signal to all the process remaining for cleaning. This may cause the command stopped in the middle of DM processing (maybe table manipulation) and the systemd-shutdown will suspended all the time if we use fsync before detach DM device. This PR is used to solve this kind of problem.

> During the shutdown process，the systemd-shutdown process will be the process 1 and send the SIGTERM and SIGKILL signal to all the process remaining for cleaning.

I hope this is the last resort when everything fails. You cannot kill udev processes that process devices teardown (like dmsetup clearing semaphore called from an udev rule, for example). This can cause not only (meta)data corruption (on several layers) but also security issues (we have to clear keys from memory etc). Clearing keys is a requirement that is not only "nice to have" but also a requirement for certifications. So please do not do this as a normal shutdown procedure.

That said, the teardown in a normal situation (no failing hw, etc.) is quick and should not block anything; it must only happen with the proper order.

I think if we're making things too complicated?

So, I guess I could accept the fact that sometimes people ask for the system to be shutdown at the wrong time, and we comply and end up in a situation like this, where some DM operation was not executed fully, and we might hang here. But if that's the case, then is checking for the target count really the right thing? From the comments of the various DM folks here I sense that this might not really be directly related.

Hence, maybe we should go a different way here:

move the fsync() call out of process. Then in the parent set a timeout. When the time-out is reached we try to kill the child, but don't bother if it fails. And then we proceed with destroying the DM without further waiting for syncing. I understand there's a way we can abruptly terminate a DM device?

> My best guess is - the DM device is simply holding IO and is not properly deactivated - for better analysis is usually good Alt+F9 systemd debug shell - that can reveal which process is blocking progress.

note that "systemd-shutdown" runs as PID 1, replacing the actual service manager, and at that time basically nothing else is running anymore. It's what we usually call the 2nd phase of shutdown, where regular service management is already over, done, finito, and we just try to robustly sync/detach/umount  whatever might still be left – but there shouldn't even be anything left here.

> Then in the parent set a timeout. When the time-out is reached we try to kill the child, but don't bother if it fails. And then we proceed with destroying the DM without further waiting for syncing. I understand there's a way we can abruptly terminate a DM device?

Globally, this is what happens when you call ``dmsetup remove_all --force`` - it tries removing all devices, if it is failing, it replaces dm-table with error target and looping again until everything is gone.  If some device cannot be still removed (due to some kernel/stuck process issue keeping it open) it is already replaced with the error target, so it can be ignored. I am not sure if we have anything that operates over sub-tree, though @zkabelac will know...
An chance we can implement that separately with just calling an ioctl or two? The "systemd-shutdown" binary is not supposed to have external deps really.

> An chance we can implement that separately with just calling an ioctl or two? The "systemd-shutdown" binary is not supposed to have external deps really.

Not sure exactly what are we trying to build - if you need to 'recreate'  logic of  'dmsetup remove_all --force' -  you would need to port this code to systemd.   There is no code in kernel space - as it doesn't belong there - so there will not be an 'ioctl()' to remove all device and replace opened one with error target.

The corresponding code is located in libdm/dm-tools/dmsetup.c _remove_all()   - but not sure whether systemd links  'libdm' or you have your own  ioctl() setup to go over this.

In essence the loop can be easily described as you go by 'list of all DM' devs' - you close those with open_count=0
Once you cannot proceed - you start replacing those with open_count=1 with 'error' target.  Ideally each such step should be hunting for mounted entries and trying to umount in forked task -  and this loop continues as far as there is any progress - once all devs are 'error' and they are still opened and there is nothing to umount - loop is finished.

Clearly devices that are in 'bad state' - i.e. due to some kernel bug - will never be destructible this way - so there always need to be implemented  some 'timeout' kernel reboot for such case..

Similar loop is implemented (with dmsetup call) in lvm2 test suite to tear down devices used in testing.

For me it's kind of unclear why this needs to be part of systemd binary - as this loop should be just a more enhanced version of 'blkdeactive.sh'  (which ATM doesn't try to use those error devs).
The only issue mandatory here is - that  systemd  flips to shutdown 'ramdisk'.

hmm, maybe to simplify things we should simply just add a timeout to the sync stuff and otherwise ignore the whole mess? i mean, syncing and then forcibly and suddenly destroying all DM devices isn't that different from syncing and turning off the power.

Hence maybe a fix for this should look like this:

Teach the existing sync_with_progress() function that it optionally takes an fd. if specified it will sync that fd, instead of just calling sync(). Then, simply use that here. That would mean we won't hang forever and otherwise we make no changes to the DM dissassembly in shutdown.c

> For me it's kind of unclear why this needs to be part of systemd binary - as this loop should be just a more enhanced version of 'blkdeactive.sh' (which ATM doesn't try to use those error devs).
> The only issue mandatory here is - that systemd flips to shutdown 'ramdisk'.

this is implemented in "systemd-shutdown" binary. Which is a single program with no deps, often compiled statically that replaces the regular service manager process as PID 1 during final shutdown phases. it is invoked at a time where *everything else* is already dead and gone. No other processes, no device management, nothing. We support it to be statically compiled because various distros copy it to a fresh tmpfs instance on shutdown, which they then can pivot into, so that they can exec it from there, so that the original rootfs is no longer reference in any way (and thus can be detached/unmounted). This little binary is supposed to clean-up everything that remains with some minimal code, robustly, time-bounded and relatively dumb. It has no deps, and definitely should never call out to external callouts or shells or anything. Hence, a DM tool to shell out out is really not an option.

(BTW; even if that wasn't that way, and we'd allow callouts there, we generally refuse new shell scripts being pulled into the boot or shutdown processes. Distros can do that, but systemd upstream is supposed to be "shell-free" in that regarded)

It seems there is possible a problem related to combination of DM on top of loop device - we will analyze this issue deeper - as a more simple reproducer one can use just:

Assuming  7:0 is a block device for our testing.

`# dmsetup create --notable xlv`
`# dmsetup load xlv --table '0 2097152 linear 7:0 2048'`

here we will have device that has PRELOADED table -  (dmsetup table --inactive)  - and now:

`# dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/dm-xxx bs=16K count=1 conv=fdatasync`

This starts to busy-loop in kernel and stops after:

`# dmsetup resume xlv`

There is just one thing to be aware of - when the system has load of RAM and some 'slower' storage - it may happen that  default linux kernel which can go over halve of RAM with dirty pages - thus it took ten minutes to synchronize everything on disk - so just to be aware there is not just 'one timeout' fits them all - it would be worth to monitor whether  dirty pages are decreasing with some time period  or there is no move - and one can assume storage is stuck.

> There is just one thing to be aware of - when the system has load of RAM and some 'slower' storage - it may happen that default linux kernel which can go over halve of RAM with dirty pages - thus it took ten minutes to synchronize everything on disk - so just to be aware there is not just 'one timeout' fits them all - it would be worth to monitor whether dirty pages are decreasing with some time period or there is no move - and one can assume storage is stuck.

https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/34330 actually should cover for that, it doesn't just wait for a time-out, it actually watches /proc/meminfo, and waits as long as NFS_Unstable/Writeback/Dirty keep shrinking. The timeout is only applied once the sum of those fields does not shrink anymore.

Under the assumption that DM's caches are covered by these three fields in one form or another we should be safe here hence.

> #34330 actually should cover for that, it doesn't just wait for a time-out, it actually watches /proc/meminfo, and waits as long as NFS_Unstable/Writeback/Dirty keep shrinking. The timeout is only applied once the sum of those fields does not shrink anymore.

Ok - this is good (was not obvious from the patch itself).  Unfortunately  DM  is not associated with page cache (dirty)  - so DM work is currently measurable mostly by checking iostats on  individual DM device - if there is some work going on - numbers are growing up -     clearly there is a problem with possibly 'busy-looping' which would generate endless IO - so some sort of timeout  may need to be set to finish such jobs.

@zkabelac humm, is there any chance we can get a single file in procfs or sysfs that returns us the "dirty" bytes over all devices? we really need something here we can easily read in userspace, in dumb code.

> @zkabelac humm, is there any chance we can get a single file in procfs or sysfs that returns us the "dirty" bytes over all devices? we really need something here we can easily read in userspace, in dumb code.

ATM I'd doubt DM team would be willing to add another kind of atomic_t  counter into the code's hot path - since there is heavy push in opposite direction to absolutely minimize any  kind extra code  (as NVMe is simply way too fast - so every extra code in IO processing counts and is very noticeable) .

However parsing and checking content of /sys/block/dm-0/stat    (or somewhat more racy one for read  /inflight) is really trivial in userspace - so IMHO a bit more annoying then checking a single sysfs entry, but still simple to add.

A simple loop iterating over  /sys/block/dm-xxx/stat - summing up  on going IO  and comparing  with last remembered value is likely something that should be mostly equivalent to checking decreasing dirty value.

> ATM I'd doubt DM team would be willing to add another kind of atomic_t counter into the code's hot path - since there is heavy push in opposite direction to absolutely minimize any kind extra code (as NVMe is simply way too fast - so every extra code in IO processing counts and is very noticeable) .

Well, it could work the other way round: when userspace reads it, it iterates through the devices and adds up the counters. i.e. i think it's fine if this is quick to update, but slow to read.

> However parsing and checking content of /sys/block/dm-0/stat (or somewhat more racy one for read /inflight) is really trivial in userspace - so IMHO a bit more annoying then checking a single sysfs entry, but still simple to add.

Hmmm, but this these counters are not a reflection on how much is still to do but more about how much is being done. Which is quite a difference, no? For this shutdown syncing we'd like to look at the pool of stuff left to do, and if we make progress there, not so much whether any IO is generated at all...

> > However parsing and checking content of /sys/block/dm-0/stat (or somewhat more racy one for read /inflight) is really trivial in userspace - so IMHO a bit more annoying then checking a single sysfs entry, but still simple to add.
> 
> Hmmm, but this these counters are not a reflection on how much is still to do but more about how much is being done. Which is quite a difference, no? For this shutdown syncing we'd like to look at the pool of stuff left to do, and if we make progress there, not so much whether any IO is generated at all...

ATM there is nothing in DM that would be even trying to estimate how much BIO would need to go to devices - most  of IO is initiated from the user-space or page cache - but it's pretty much unknown how much IO this may generate on DM level - only few targets can probably estimate how much write is ahead of them - i.e. writecache synchronizing to origin device.

So really all you can mostly get is whether there is some 'write' traffic still going on at  those 'stat' information'  -  'read' traffic should be mostly ignored for the 'shutdown' purpose.

It's probably worth to note that in major use case - 'empty dirty pages' should mostly signals that DM devices should be almost always also in quiet state -  ideally such devices should be 'closed & removed from DM table'.

Checking for  'writing'  in this cases should be mostly for peace of mind.

There are although cases  - where 'deactivation' should be preferred way to solve the issue - i.e. raid leg synchronization - so when  raid1  is synchronizing   dm-001  ->  dm-002  - that may potentially be an operation taking hours/days for large devices - and here reboot clearly shouldn't  be waiting that long -   especially when user 'band-limits' write throughput for synchronization.

So not sure what all is systemd-shutdown  doing - but 'deactivation' should be always the most preferred variant - and this aborting in-the-middle  should be made only as the last 'resort'  (and surely  raid1 LV  will restart it's synchronization task nicely after reboot)

> > My suggesion for a fix is waiting in #34330. PTAL.
> 
> This fix has been merged in the meantime. @huyubiao any chance you can see if your system is able to shutdown properly within bounded time, with that PR applied?

Thanks.  The system can be shutdown within bounded time.

issue_context.title: systemd-shutdown hang all the timen (if DM devices with no targets exist)
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

255

### Used distribution

Fedora 39

### Linux kernel version used

kernel-6.6.0-136.x86_64

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

None

### Component

systemd

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

The computer is shut down or restarted.

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

systemd-shutdown hang all the time

### Steps to reproduce the problem

During the shutdown, all DMs are detached. The fsync_path_at() is delivered , and then the ioctl() is executed to delete the DMs. However, the DMs are hanged in the fsync:
```
static int delete_dm(DeviceMapper *m) {
...
        r = fsync_path_at(AT_FDCWD, m->path);
        if (r < 0)
                log_debug_errno(r, "Failed to sync DM block device %s, ignoring: %m", m->path);

        return RET_NERRNO(ioctl(fd, DM_DEV_REMOVE, &(struct dm_ioctl) {
...
}
```
According to the dm device information parsed by the vmcore, the dm has been created successfully, but the mapping table has not been loaded. The I/O delivered by the fsync is delayed. However, the systemd-shutdown process has been started and all processes are stopped,and the mapping table cannot be loaded. As a result, the I/O is suspended, and systemd-shutdown is hanged as well.

In addition to /dev/watchdog(The /dev/watchdog and the /dev/watchdog0 device does not exist on my machine), are there any other methods that can prevent the system from being stuck? ()
Or check whether the DM mapping table exists before fsync()?



### Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue

_No response_
comments:
I prepped an fix in #34330, that should address the issue here. It's entirely generic and puts a global timeout on any kind of fsync() we issue from the shutdown binary. It does not try to be smart in anyway, but that's a good ting, and should mean we won't hang unbounded here.

As I understand this is triggered by a local mishandling of the device. I think it#s hence fine if we handle this via a timeout here. We don't have to try to be "clean" in shutdown.c because the triggering condition isn't clean either.
Aynway, would be great if you could check if #34330 makes the issue go away for you?

> Aynway, would be great if you could check if #34330 makes the issue go away for you?

Thanks. The system can be shutdown within bounded time. Close this issue.
